content: 1. Vial stoppers used in the packaging of this medication are not made with natural rubber latex, reducing the risk of allergic reactions in sensitive individuals. 2. This medication is indicated as a complete regimen for the treatment of HIV-1 infection in adults and adolescents. It is specifically intended for patients who are virologically suppressed (HIV-1 RNA < 50 copies/mL), have no history of treatment failure, and have no known or suspected resistance to cabotegravir or rilpivirine. 3. The regimen may be initiated with an optional oral lead-in therapy for at least 28 days or administered directly as an injection. 4. For adolescents aged 12 years or older and weighing at least 35 kg, the safety and efficacy of this regimen have been established. However, it is not recommended for children under 12 years of age, as safety and efficacy data are lacking. 5. Carbamazepine decreases rilpivirine levels by inducing hepatic and intestinal CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated due to the risk of virologic failure and potential resistance to rilpivirine or the NNRTI class. 6. Dexamethasone also decreases rilpivirine levels via CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated for the same reasons as carbamazepine. 7. Rilpivirine should not be co-administered with strong CYP3A4 inducers, as this may lead to a loss of virologic response and resistance to rilpivirine or the NNRTI class. 8. Dexlansoprazole increases gastric pH, reducing rilpivirine levels. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Co-administration is contraindicated due to the risk of treatment failure and resistance. 9. Efavirenz decreases rilpivirine levels via CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated, and rilpivirine should not be used in combination with other NNRTIs. 10. Elvitegravir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir DF is a complete regimen for HIV and should not be co-administered with other antiretrovirals, including rilpivirine. 11. Eslicarbazepine acetate decreases rilpivirine levels via CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated due to the risk of virologic failure and resistance. 12. Esomeprazole increases gastric pH, reducing rilpivirine levels. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Co-administration is contraindicated due to the risk of treatment failure and resistance. 13. Etravirine decreases rilpivirine levels via CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated, and rilpivirine should not be used in combination with other NNRTIs. 14. Fosphenytoin decreases rilpivirine levels via CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated due to the risk of virologic failure and resistance. 15. Lansoprazole increases gastric pH, reducing rilpivirine levels. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Co-administration is contraindicated due to the risk of treatment failure and resistance. 16. Nevirapine decreases rilpivirine levels via CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated, and rilpivirine should not be used in combination with other NNRTIs. 17. Omeprazole increases gastric pH, reducing rilpivirine levels. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Co-administration is contraindicated due to the risk of treatment failure and resistance. 18. Oxcarbazepine decreases rilpivirine levels via CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated due to the risk of virologic failure and resistance. 19. Pantoprazole increases gastric pH, reducing rilpivirine levels. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Co-administration is contraindicated due to the risk of treatment failure and resistance. 20. Phenobarbital decreases rilpivirine levels via CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated due to the risk of virologic failure and resistance. 21. Phenytoin decreases rilpivirine levels via CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated due to the risk of virologic failure and resistance. 22. Rabeprazole increases gastric pH, reducing rilpivirine levels. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Co-administration is contraindicated due to the risk of treatment failure and resistance. 23. Rifampin decreases rilpivirine levels via CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated due to the risk of virologic failure and resistance. 24. Rifapentine decreases rilpivirine levels via CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated due to the risk of virologic failure and resistance. 25. St. John’s Wort decreases rilpivirine levels via CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated due to the risk of virologic failure and resistance. 26. Vonoprazan decreases rilpivirine levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Co-administration is contraindicated. 27. Adagrasib and rilpivirine both prolong the QTc interval, increasing the risk of torsades de pointes and other serious arrhythmias. Co-administration should be avoided or alternative drugs should be used. If unavoidable, frequent ECG monitoring is recommended. 28. Amisulpride and rilpivirine both prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided or alternative drugs should be used. ECG monitoring is recommended if co-administered. 29. Anagrelide and rilpivirine both prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided or alternative drugs should be used. 30. Artemether and rilpivirine both prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided or alternative drugs should be used. 31. Rilpivirine and atidarsagene autotemcel may interfere with each other. Antiretroviral medications should not be taken for at least one month before cell mobilization or during the expected duration of medication elimination. 32. Bedaquiline and rilpivirine both prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided or alternative drugs should be used. 33. Rilpivirine and betibeglogene autotemcel may interfere with each other. Antiretroviral medications should not be taken for at least one month before mobilization and until all apheresis cycles are completed. 34. Buprenorphine (all forms) and rilpivirine both prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided or alternative drugs should be used. 35. Ceritinib and rilpivirine both prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided or alternative drugs should be used. 36. Desflurane and rilpivirine both prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided or alternative drugs should be used. 37. Dofetilide increases rilpivirine toxicity by prolonging the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided or alternative drugs should be used. 38. Efavirenz and rilpivirine both prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided or alternative drugs should be used. 39. Elivaldogene autotemcel and rilpivirine may interfere with each other. Antiretroviral medications should not be taken for at least one month before initiating stem cell mobilization medications. 40. Encorafenib and rilpivirine both prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided or alternative drugs should be used. 41. Entrectinib and rilpivirine both prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided or alternative drugs should be used. 42. Eribulin and rilpivirine both prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided or alternative drugs should be used. 43. Fexinidazole and rilpivirine both prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided or alternative drugs should be used. Avoid combining fexinidazole with drugs that block potassium channels or prolong the QT interval. 44. Rilpivirine and givinostat both prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided or alternative drugs should be used. If unavoidable, obtain ECGs at baseline, during concomitant use, and as clinically indicated. Withhold treatment if the QTc interval exceeds 500 ms or if there is a change from baseline greater than 60 ms. 45. Hydroxychloroquine sulfate and rilpivirine both prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided or alternative drugs should be used. 46. Isoflurane and rilpivirine both prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided or alternative drugs should be used. 47. Lefamulin and rilpivirine both prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided or alternative drugs should be used. 48. Rilpivirine and lovotibeglogene autotemcel may interfere with each other. Discontinue antiretrovirals at least one month before mobilization and until all apheresis cycles are completed. Some long-acting antiretrovirals may require a longer discontinuation period for elimination. 49. Macimorelin and rilpivirine both prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided or alternative drugs should be used. Macimorelin increases the QT interval by approximately 11 ms. Allow sufficient washout time of QT-prolonging drugs before administering macimorelin. 50. Ombitasvir/paritaprevir/ritonavir and dasabuvir (DSC) increase rilpivirine levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is not recommended due to the potential for QT interval prolongation with higher rilpivirine concentrations. 51. Oxaliplatin and rilpivirine both prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided or alternative drugs should be used. 52. Ribociclib increases rilpivirine toxicity by prolonging the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided or alternative drugs should be used. 53. Rifabutin decreases rilpivirine levels via CYP3A4 metabolism. If co-administered, increase rilpivirine dose to 50 mg once daily. When rifabutin is stopped, decrease rilpivirine dose to 25 mg once daily. 54. Sevoflurane and rilpivirine both prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided or alternative drugs should be used. 55. Siponimod and rilpivirine both prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided or alternative drugs should be used. 56. Tetrabenazine and rilpivirine both prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided or alternative drugs should be used. 57. Tovorafenib decreases rilpivirine levels via CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration should be avoided or alternative drugs should be used. If unavoidable, monitor patients for loss of efficacy. 58. Rilpivirine increases the toxicity of umeclidinium bromide/vilanterol inhaled by prolonging the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided or alternative drugs should be used. Exercise caution when vilanterol is co-administered with QT-prolonging drugs. 59. Rilpivirine increases the toxicity of vilanterol/fluticasone furoate inhaled by prolonging the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided or alternative drugs should be used. Exercise caution when vilanterol is co-administered with QT-prolonging drugs. 60. Albuterol and rilpivirine both prolong the QTc interval. Use caution and monitor patients closely. 61. Rilpivirine increases the toxicity of amiodarone by prolonging the QTc interval. Use caution and monitor patients closely. 62. Rilpivirine increases the toxicity of amitriptyline by prolonging the QTc interval. Use caution and monitor patients closely. 63. Rilpivirine increases the toxicity of amoxapine by prolonging the QTc interval. Use caution and monitor patients closely. 64. Rilpivirine increases the toxicity of apomorphine by prolonging the QTc interval. Use caution and monitor patients closely.
